summary:
Georgia's own law and practice diverge from the national layer in ways a trans visitor should weigh. Care for minors is banned by statute, the state employee health plan is under a court settlement requiring it to pay for gender-affirming care, and access to adult surgery narrowed abruptly in Savannah in 2025. Documented violence against transgender women in the state has centred on Atlanta.

Senate Bill 140, signed by Governor Brian Kemp on 23 March 2023 and in force since 1 July 2023, bars licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or surgery for gender transition to patients under 18. Licence revocation is a possible penalty. Minors who began hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue under the law. The ACLU of Georgia said it would sue.

A settlement announced in October 2023 in federal court in Atlanta requires Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, their spouses and their dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit alleged the plan illegally discriminated by refusing to pay. The plan's coverage of minors' care can extend to treatment obtained outside Georgia, even though that care is prohibited inside the state. The settlement keeps public-employee coverage in place alongside the 2023 ban.

Atlanta police said in April 2023 that they were investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. The department described the violence against Black and Brown transgender women as epidemic-level. The sourcing gives raw counts without a denominator for the city's general homicide rate, so the figures establish that these attacks occurred and were under investigation, not that transgender residents face a risk measurably above the background rate of violence in the city.

Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on 13 February 2025, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man. The hospital cited a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations, and the cancellation came in the weeks after a January 2025 federal order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care.
tangentialFactors:
The two care rules pull in opposite directions for state employees. Georgia law prohibits licensed professionals in the state from providing transition-related hormone therapy or surgery to under-18 patients, while the health plan settlement obliges the plan to pay for medically necessary care for dependents, and can require it for minors treated out of state. A family covered by the plan therefore has a payment route for care that cannot lawfully be delivered by a Georgia-licensed clinician.

Adult surgical capacity in Georgia turns partly on funding decisions taken outside the state. Memorial Health's February 2025 cancellation cited compliance with state and federal law and followed a federal funding directive aimed at youth transition care, yet the surgeries withdrawn included a procedure for a 24-year-old adult.
localsOnly:
Residents under 18 cannot lawfully receive transition-related hormone therapy or surgery from a Georgia-licensed professional; those already on hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue. Clinicians who provide the prohibited care risk losing their licence.

State employees, their spouses and dependents enrolled in the State Health Benefit Plan have coverage for medically necessary gender-affirming care under the October 2023 settlement, a coverage line that survived the 2023 statutory ban.

Residents of the Savannah area lost access to gender-affirming surgery when Memorial Health University Medical Center cancelled all such procedures on 13 February 2025. Savannah Pride Center said at least two people besides the 24-year-old whose pre-approved double mastectomy was cancelled were also denied care.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation the ACLU of Georgia announced against Senate Bill 140 is not established in the sourcing, and the ban's current enforceability should be verified before travel.

The sourcing does not record whether Memorial Health's suspension of gender-affirming surgery is permanent, nor whether other Georgia hospital systems have taken similar steps; Savannah is the only documented instance of adult surgical capacity contracting in the state.

No per-capita or comparative data on violence against transgender people in Georgia appears in the sourcing, and the outcome of the three Atlanta investigations reported in April 2023 is not recorded.

How far the health plan settlement is applied in practice, including whether the plan pays for minors' care obtained out of state, is not sourced beyond the terms of the settlement itself.
